en.g: Io, 85 Io, a large asteroid in the asteroid belt

1000483.etyen:
Internationalism, borrowed from Latin Īō (“Io”), from Ancient Greek Ἰώ (Iṓ, “Io”), itself of Pre-Greek origin. The meaning and ultimate origin of the Pre-Greek name are unknown.
The astronomical names derive from the mythological figure. Simon Marius proposed the name Io for Jupiter's innermost Galilean moon in 1614, following a suggestion by Johannes Kepler that the four moons be named after mythological figures associated with Jupiter. 1001763.etyen:
Nominalization of god morgen (“good morning”), written as one word. The underlying greeting consists of god (“good”) and morgen (“morning”), literally “good morning”.
The first element continues Old Norse góðr (“good”), from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz (“good, suitable”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to unite; to fit, suit”). The second reflects Danish morgen (“morning”), from Old Danish morghæn (“morning”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *murginaz (“morning”), also reconstructed with other second-syllable vowels.

1005091.etyen:
The exact formation is uncertain. According to Store norske leksikon, Anine may be derived from one of the female given names Anna, Anne or Ane. Nordic Names instead treats it as a variant of Anina, itself a Romance diminutive of Anna. First attested in the c. 1790.
The name belongs to the Anna name family, ultimately from Late Latin Anna, from Koine Greek Ἄννα (Ánna), from Biblical Hebrew חַנָּה (Ḥannāh, “Hannah; grace, favour”).
Compare Danish Anine and Swedish Anine (“female given name”).
